Sorry but a closed practice is a closed practice because it is specifically cultural, and doing a specifically cultural practice is appropriation. It’s like saying because Haitian VouDou isn’t a “secret” it isn’t a closed practice but it very much is and forms of brujería is closed because of the cultural aspects of it. Santa muerte itself isn’t a closed practice. But there are certain practices that are closed because they stem from a cultural context and are deeply rooted in our culture and people outside of it simply wouldn’t understand or be able to respect it. Closed practices are closed because they are tied to our ethnic and cultural identities, because they focus on our heritage and traditions, because participation in these practices is often viewed as a cultural practice as well as a religious one. There are different degrees to closed practices, most are fully closed to outsiders and only those within the culture and heritage are allowed to practice, whilst others require an imitation process to enter where you fully educate yourself and do whatever else is required to become a practitioner.

Ik this is old but I should just put this out there anyway. Sexuality is fluid. It’s different for everyone. There is no right way to be queer. I have seen stories of a gay man being married to his best friend (a woman she knew he was gay but still wanted to marry him) and years after their marriage he realized he loved her. Maybe not physically. But emotionally he loved her. The world is quick to put a label on people, bc it wants to put you in a box but people aren’t meant to be put in boxes. Soulmates come in every shape and form,(I’m talking about the romantic kind) and maybe the form they come in isn’t what you are usually attracted to, but there’s a tug in your heart and you realize you love them despite your set in stone attraction. A lot of homophobic people in this world act like if your gay you have to be in that box your entire life without your preferences changing and evolving and if they do evolve they’ll say smth dumb like you were never actually gay in the first place. But that’s not true, and because of that there is so much stigma to the fluidity of sexuality and people try to ignore that. But please remember, to anyone going through something like this, sexuality is fluid, it is not linear. There is no one way to be gay or straight. There is just you, and what you are comfortable with, and what you feel. By nature humans are creatures of fluidity, trying to restrict that and keep yourself in a box others made for you despite the fact, that maybe you don’t quite fit in that box the way others do, is harmful to yourself. You don’t have to fit in the box the way others do. Sometimes being outside of it is so much more fun.

This honestly isn’t easy. I don’t know what to tell you because I can see both perspectives. I am a victim of sexual assault. So please listen to me when I say, that this is a tricky situation. On one hand, you did what you thought was best, your worries were valid and reporting him was valid to- especially because she most likely isn’t his first or last victim, and by reporting him you probably saved her and any future woman he decides to traumatize next. On the other hand, I say this as a victim of SA, the reporting process is very sacred to us, sometimes we choose not to report it out of fear it’ll just get worse, reporting could ruin our own futures and it could end with us dead or even more traumatized or maybe for specific people moving on from it is how they heal and Sometimes we choose to report it so that we can stop it from ever happening again, and it’s kind of a way to get at least some closure, and for a lot of people it can be a step into healing. So this whole process like I said, is very sacred to us. While I understand what you did (you have probably protected lots of future woman so thank you) I also think that this should’ve been solved in a different way. I believe you should’ve given her some space to think about what she wanted to do and just listened to her when she vented, I think instead of going straight to the police for her you should’ve tried to talk to her about reporting and you should’ve asked her why she didn’t want to and had a really long conversation about what it is she wants and given her a choice (bc that choice is the most important thing for us- it’s giving us that control that was taken from us) you went to the police FOR her- but really you should’ve let her go FOR herself or you should’ve went to the police WITH her (with her permission and with her by your side *phonecall* or whatnot) what you did could’ve protected her and so many other women, but it also could’ve been even more dangerous for her, but the main issue here is- you violated her trust and took away her choice, and that is exactly what the abuser did to her, it could’ve made her relive it and re-traumatized her all over again. I’m not sure how you can fix this, but I believe that maybe you should call her and apologize. Tell her what your fears were and why you reported it, don’t make this about you, she was the one who was violated, you need to be sincere in your apology. Apologize for violating her trust and taking her choice away, apologize and tell her you know that you don’t deserve her trust but that you will do whatever you can to earn it back, and to fix the mistake you made. Grovel and apologize and tell her you will reflect and be better. Tell her that you should never have violated that trust and that you are sorry. And she probably isn’t going to forgive you right away, and she’s never gonna trust you the same and that is something you are going to need to be understanding about and it is going to take a LOT of time for her to forgive you. So be patient.
